pattern: Behavioral finance applies behavioral psychology to investment decisions, revealing systematic deviations from rational pricing. Key phenomena: (1) Loss Aversion — losses hurt ~2x more than equivalent gains please, leading to risk asymmetry: holding losing positions too long (hope of break-even) while selling winners too early (locking in gains); (2) Disposition Effect — correlated with loss aversion; investors sell winners quickly (realizing gains) but hold losers (avoiding realizing loss), creating tax inefficiency and suboptimal portfolios; (3) Herding — following the crowd rather than independent analysis, amplified by social proof and fear of missing out; explains bubbles and crashes as self-reinforcing collective behavior; (4) Overconfidence — traders overestimate their information quality and predictive ability, leading to excessive trading, higher turnover, and lower net returns after costs; (5) Mental Accounting — segregating money into non-fungible accounts (retirement vs. vacation fund vs. 'play money'), causing irrational allocation decisions that ignore total wealth optimization. These patterns explain why markets are not efficiently priced and why many investors underperform their benchmarks.
source: Wikipedia: Behavioral finance — Thaler, Kahneman, Tversky, Shiller

description: People evaluate outcomes relative to a reference point, not absolute wealth. The value function is S-shaped: concave for gains (risk-averse), convex for losses (risk-seeking), and steeper for losses than gains.

examples.observation: Most reject — loss aversion coefficient λ≈2.3 means -$100 feels like -$230, while +$110 feels like +$110. Net: -120 perceived value vs. +5 EV.

trading_implications: Disposition effect: sell winners too early (lock in gains), hold losers too long (avoid realizing losses)
Framing matters: same outcome described as '90% survival' vs. '10% mortality' changes decisions
Reference point is subjective: entry price, 52-week high, or breakeven all serve as anchors

pattern: Predictive processing (predictive coding) is a Bayesian framework where perception is active inference — the brain constantly generates top-down predictions about sensory input and updates them via prediction errors. Key concepts: (1) Hierarchical generative models at multiple timescales (fast perceptual inference vs slow learning); (2) Prediction errors propagate upward, predictions flow downward; (3) Free energy minimization — the system minimizes surprise by updating internal models or acting on the world; (4) Active inference: action is belief-driven sampling of sensory data to confirm predictions; (5) Precision weighting — attention is allocating computational resources to high-precision prediction errors. This contrasts with traditional feedforward models (stimulus → response) by making perception inherently inferential and action-oriented. Applications: perception, motor control, learning, attention disorders (autism, schizophrenia).
source: Wikipedia: Free energy principle, Predictive coding — Friston, Clark, Hohwy

Shannon entropy quantifies the average uncertainty in a random variable. Formula: H(X) = -sum(p(x) * log2(p(x))) for all outcomes x. Key properties: (1) H(X) >= 0, equals 0 only when one outcome has probability 1 (no uncertainty); (2) Maximum entropy occurs when all outcomes are equally likely — H(X) = log2(n) for n outcomes; (3) Entropy is additive for independent variables: H(X,Y) = H(X) + H(Y); (4) Conditional entropy H(X|Y) = H(X,Y) - H(Y) measures uncertainty in X remaining after observing Y; (5) Joint entropy H(X,Y) = H(X) + H(Y|Y) = H(Y) + H(X|Y). Intuition: entropy is the average number of bits needed to encode outcomes of X under optimal compression. A fair coin has entropy 1 bit; a biased coin (90/10) has entropy ~0.47 bits. Applications: data compression limits (no lossless scheme beats entropy), feature importance (high-entropy features carry more information), model uncertainty (predictive distributions with high entropy indicate model ignorance), sensor data quality (low-entropy sensor streams are redundant). Connection to ML: cross-entropy loss H(p,q) = -sum(p(x)*log(q(x))) measures how many bits we use when encoding true distribution p using model distribution q — always >= H(p) with equality when p=q.

Kullback-Leibler divergence measures how one probability distribution differs from a reference distribution. Formula: D_KL(p || q) = sum(p(x) * log(p(x)/q(x))) for all x. Key properties: (1) Not symmetric: D_KL(p||q) != D_KL(q||p) — direction matters; (2) Always >= 0 (Gibbs' inequality), equals 0 iff p=q everywhere; (3) Relates to entropy: D_KL(p||q) = H(p,q) - H(p), the excess bits from using q to encode p; (4) Satisfies triangle inequality when symmetrized (Jensen-Shannon divergence); (5) Additive for independent variables. Intuition: KL divergence is the 'surprise cost' of using the wrong model. If the true distribution is p but you encode with q, you waste D_KL(p||q) extra bits per symbol on average. Applications: (a) Model comparison — lower KL means better fit; (b) Variational inference — minimize KL between approximate and posterior distributions; (c) Reinforcement learning — policy gradient as KL minimization; (d) Sensor calibration — KL between expected and observed distributions quantifies calibration drift; (e) Feature selection — KL divergence between joint and marginal distributions equals mutual information. Connection to predictive processing: prediction error minimization IS KL divergence minimization — the brain minimizes D_KL between predicted and actual sensory distributions.

Mutual information quantifies statistical dependence between two random variables. Formula: I(X;Y) = sum(p(x,y) * log(p(x,y)/(p(x)*p(y)))) = H(X) - H(X|Y) = H(Y) - H(Y|X) = H(X) + H(Y) - H(X,Y). Key properties: (1) Symmetric: I(X;Y) = I(Y;X); (2) Always >= 0, equals 0 iff X and Y are independent; (3) Bounded by individual entropies: I(X;Y) <= min(H(X), H(Y)); (4) Chain rule: I(X;Y,Z) = I(X;Y) + I(X;Z|Y). Intuition: mutual information is the reduction in uncertainty about X gained by observing Y. If X and Y are perfectly correlated, I(X;Y) = H(X) = H(Y). If independent, I(X;Y) = 0. Applications: (a) Feature selection — select features with highest MI with target variable; (b) Channel capacity — C = max over input distributions of I(X;Y), the Shannon-Hartley theorem; (c) Clustering — maximize MI between data and cluster assignments; (d) Neuroscience — quantify information flow between brain regions; (e) NLP — word association strength via pointwise mutual information PMI(x,y) = log(p(x,y)/(p(x)*p(y))); (f) Sensor fusion — MI between sensors tells you how much new information each additional sensor provides. Connection to governance: MI between pattern categories could quantify how interconnected my knowledge base is — low MI means siloed knowledge, high MI means cross-pollinated understanding.

Rate-distortion theory determines the trade-off between data compression rate and acceptable reconstruction error. Core concept: given a source with entropy H, what is the minimum bit rate R needed to reconstruct within distortion D? The rate-distortion function R(D) = min over all channels with expected distortion <= D of I(X;Y̅). Key properties: (1) R(D) is monotonically decreasing — more distortion allows lower rate; (2) R(0) = H(X) — perfect reconstruction requires full entropy; (3) R(H(X)) = 0 — ignoring all information gives zero rate; (4) For Gaussian sources with MSE distortion: R(D) = 0.5 * log2(sigma²/D). Intuition: you don't always need perfect reconstruction. JPEG, MP3, and video codecs all operate on rate-distortion principles — they keep the bits that matter most to human perception and discard the rest. The optimal codec allocates more bits to perceptually important features (edges in images, harmonics in audio) and fewer to noise-like content. Applications: (a) Lossy compression — JPEG, MP3, H.264 all optimize rate-distortion trade-offs; (b) Sensor data logging — sample at full resolution, compress with perceptual distortion threshold; (c) Memory management — store high-entropy patterns at full fidelity, compress low-entropy observations; (d) Communication under bandwidth constraints — ESP32 sensor data could use rate-distortion optimization to minimize transmission while maintaining calibration accuracy. Connection to cognition: the brain is a rate-distortion optimizer — it compresses sensory input to minimal representation while preserving behaviorally relevant information.

Bayes' theorem is the fundamental law of probabilistic reasoning — updating beliefs in light of evidence. Formula: P(H|E) = P(E|H) * P(H) / P(E). Components: (1) Prior P(H) — belief in hypothesis H before seeing evidence; (2) Likelihood P(E|H) — probability of observing evidence E if H is true; (3) Marginal P(E) = sum over all hypotheses of P(E|Hi)*P(Hi) — normalization ensuring probabilities sum to 1; (4) Posterior P(H|E) — updated belief after incorporating evidence. Log-space formulation (computationally stable): log P(H|E) = log P(E|H) + log P(H) - log P(E). Iterative updating: today's posterior becomes tomorrow's prior — P(H|E1,E2) = P(E2|H,E1) * P(H|E1) / P(E2|E1). This is sequential belief revision, the mathematical core of learning. Key insight: Bayes' theorem doesn't tell you what prior to use — it tells you how to update whatever prior you have. The prior encodes assumptions; the data encodes reality. The posterior is the compromise. Connection to information theory: the KL divergence between prior and posterior, D_KL(posterior || prior), measures the information gain from observing evidence — exactly the mutual information I(H;E). Connection to predictive processing: prediction error is the log-likelihood ratio log P(E|H_true) / P(E|H_model); minimizing prediction error IS maximizing posterior probability. Applications: (a) Medical diagnosis — update disease probability given test results; (b) Spam filtering — update spam probability given word features; (c) A/B testing — update conversion rate probability given observed clicks; (d) Sensor fusion — update state estimate given noisy measurements; (e) Quant signals — update probability that a trade will be profitable given market conditions.

Conjugate priors are probability distributions that, when combined with likelihood and normalized, yield a posterior in the same family — enabling analytical (closed-form) Bayesian updates without numerical integration. The conjugacy relationship: Prior in family F + Likelihood L → Posterior in family F. Common conjugate pairs: (1) Beta-Binomial: Beta(α,β) prior on probability p, binomial likelihood → Beta(α+k, β+n-k) posterior where k=successes, n=trials. Parameters update additively — α counts imaginary successes, β counts imaginary failures; (2) Normal-Normal: Normal(μ₀, σ₀²) prior on mean μ, normal likelihood with known variance → Normal(μₙ, σₙ²) posterior. Precision (1/variance) adds: 1/σₙ² = 1/σ₀² + n/σ². The posterior mean is a weighted average of prior mean and sample mean, weighted by precision; (3) Gamma-Poisson: Gamma(α,β) prior on rate λ, Poisson likelihood → Gamma(α+k, β+t) posterior where k=events, t=time; (4) Normal-Gamma: Normal-Gamma prior on (μ, σ²) → Normal-Gamma posterior. Joint estimation of mean and variance; (5) Dirichlet-Multinomial: Dirichlet(α) prior on categorical probabilities, multinomial likelihood → Dirichlet(α+k) posterior. Generalizes Beta to multiple categories. Key insight: conjugate priors make Bayesian updating a bookkeeping exercise — you just add observed counts to prior pseudo-counts. This is computationally efficient and interpretable: the prior is a statement about how much fake data you've seen. Connection to information theory: the posterior entropy H(posterior) <= H(prior), with reduction equal to mutual information between parameter and data. Connection to sensor calibration: each sensor reading updates the calibration parameters via conjugate update — no need to retrain from scratch, just incrementally refine. Applications: (a) Online A/B testing — Beta-Binomial updates conversion rate after each observation; (b) Sensor calibration — Normal-Normal updates sensor offset with each reading; (c) Rate estimation — Gamma-Poisson updates failure rate with each event; (d) Topic modeling — Dirichlet-Multinomial updates topic distributions.

Empirical Bayes and hierarchical Bayesian models address the prior selection problem by estimating priors from data rather than choosing them subjectively. Empirical Bayes (EB): estimate prior parameters from the marginal data distribution. Method: (1) Assume prior P(θ|φ) with hyperparameters φ; (2) Estimate φ by maximizing marginal likelihood P(data|φ) = integral of P(data|θ)*P(θ|φ) dθ; (3) Use estimated prior to compute posteriors. This is the method of moments or maximum marginal likelihood approach. Example: estimating baseball batting averages. Instead of uniform prior (ignores that most players bat ~.250), EB estimates a Beta prior from the distribution of all players' averages, then shrinks each player's estimate toward the population mean. The shrinkage amount depends on sample size — players with few at-bats shrink more, veterans with many at-bats shrink less. Hierarchical Bayes: full Bayesian treatment where hyperparameters φ have their own prior P(φ), creating a hierarchy: data → θ → φ. This propagates uncertainty about the prior into the posterior, avoiding the overconfidence of point-estimate EB. Key insight: hierarchical models enable partial pooling — estimates borrow strength across groups without assuming they're identical (complete pooling) or independent (no pooling). This is the Goldilocks zone between ignoring group structure and overfitting to each group. Connection to information theory: the hierarchical prior's entropy encodes the diversity of the population. High entropy prior = diverse population, low shrinkage. Low entropy prior = homogeneous population, strong shrinkage. The mutual information between groups measures how much knowing one group's parameters tells you about others. Connection to governance: pattern categories across my knowledge base can be modeled hierarchically — each pattern belongs to a category, categories have distributions over topics. Hierarchical Bayes would estimate the category-topic distribution from all patterns, then use it to inform new pattern classification. Applications: (a) Multi-arm bandits — estimate reward distributions across arms with shared prior; (b) Meta-analysis — combine study results with hierarchical model of effect sizes; (c) Recommender systems — estimate user preferences with population-level priors; (d) Multi-agent coordination — estimate co-agent capabilities from observed behavior, sharing priors across agents.
source: Good 1950, Morris 1983, Gelman hierarchical modeling, Wikipedia: Empirical Bayes

pattern: Bayesian model comparison selects between competing hypotheses using posterior probabilities rather than point estimates. Given models M₁, M₂, ..., Mₖ with observed data D: (1) Posterior model probability: P(Mᵢ|D) = P(D|Mᵢ) * P(Mᵢ) / sumⱼ P(D|Mⱼ) * P(Mⱼ); (2) Marginal likelihood (evidence): P(D|Mᵢ) = integral of P(D|θ,Mᵢ) * P(θ|Mᵢ) dθ — averages over all parameter values weighted by prior; (3) Bayes factor: BF₁₂ = P(D|M₁) / P(D|M₂) — the evidence ratio. Interpretation (Jeffreys scale): BF > 1 favors M₁, BF > 3 substantial, BF > 10 strong, BF > 30 very strong. Key property: marginal likelihood automatically penalizes model complexity (Occam's razor). A complex model spreads its prior over many parameter values, diluting its average predictive accuracy. A simple model concentrates its predictions, scoring higher if correct but lower if wrong. This is the Bayesian solution to overfitting — no regularization parameter needed, the math handles it. Approximation methods when integrals are intractable: (a) BIC: log P(D|M) ≈ log L(θ_MLE) - k/2 * log(n), where k=parameters, n=samples; (b) LOO-CV (leave-one-out cross-validation) via Pareto-smoothed importance sampling; (c) WAIC (Watanabe-Aikikake information criterion) — Bayesian alternative to AIC using full posterior. Connection to information theory: marginal likelihood relates to entropy. The log evidence log P(D|M) = H(prior) + KL(posterior || prior) - log Z, decomposing into prior entropy, information gain, and normalization. The Bayes factor is the difference in log evidence, which is the difference in average surprise under each model. Connection to predictive processing: the brain compares multiple generative models (hypotheses about the world) and weights predictions by each model's posterior probability — model evidence IS prediction accuracy. Connection to quant: comparing trading strategies (momentum vs mean-reversion vs QAE-enhanced) is model comparison. The Bayes factor tells you which strategy's edge is more likely real versus noise. Applications: (a) Model selection — choose between competing ML architectures; (b) Hypothesis testing — compare treatment vs control without p-values; (c) Strategy comparison — evaluate which trading regime explanation fits data best; (d) Feature selection — compare models with/without each feature via evidence ratio.
source: Jeffreys 1961, Kass & Raftery 1995, Watanabe 2013, Wikipedia: Bayes factor

pattern: Variational inference approximates intractable Bayesian posteriors by optimizing a simple distribution to match the true posterior. The problem: exact inference requires computing the marginal likelihood P(x|D) = integral P(x,θ|D)dθ — a high-dimensional integral with no closed form for most models. Variational inference transforms integration into optimization. Core idea: approximate the true posterior p(θ|x) with a tractable distribution q(θ) from a parameterized family, and find the q that minimizes KL divergence to the true posterior. The ELBO (Evidence Lower BOund): log P(x) = KL(q(θ) || p(θ|x)) + ELBO(q), where ELBO(q) = E_q[log p(x,θ)] - E_q[log q(θ)] = E_q[log p(x|θ)] - KL(q(θ) || p(θ)). Maximizing ELBO is equivalent to minimizing KL divergence — the two terms partition the log evidence. The ELBO has an intuitive interpretation: it's the expected log-joint minus the entropy of the approximation, balancing fit (how well q explains the data) and complexity (how spread out q is). Mean-field approximation: assume q factorizes over latent variables — q(θ₁,θ₂,...,θₖ) = q₁(θ₁) * q₂(θ₂) * ... * qₖ(θₖ). This makes each factor independent, turning a joint optimization into k independent optimizations. Coordinate Ascent VI (CAVI): update each factor qⱼ while holding others fixed. The update rule: qⱼ*(θⱼ) ∝ exp(E_{q₋ⱼ}[log p(x,θ)]), the exponential of the expected log-joint under all other factors. Iterate until convergence — each step monotonically increases ELBO. Key insight: the optimal qⱼ depends on the expected sufficient statistics of the other factors, creating a message-passing structure similar to belief propagation. Variational inference vs sampling: VI is deterministic and fast (optimization), MCMC is stochastic and asymptotically exact (sampling). VI underestimates uncertainty (single mode approximation), MCMC captures full posterior but is slow. For most practical applications, VI's speed-accuracy trade-off wins. Connection to information theory: VI IS KL divergence minimization (C520). The ELBO decomposition log P(x) = KL + ELBO shows that evidence = approximation error + lower bound. The entropy term in ELBO, H(q), encourages exploration — without it, q would collapse to a delta function maximizing likelihood. Connection to Bayesian inference: VI makes Bayesian inference scalable. Where conjugate priors (C521) give exact updates for simple models, VI gives approximate updates for complex models — hierarchical models, latent Dirichlet allocation, Bayesian neural networks. Applications: (a) Bayesian neural networks — approximate weight posteriors for uncertainty quantification; (b) Topic modeling (LDA) — infer topic distributions over documents via mean-field VI; (c) Probabilistic programming — automatic inference in Stan, PyMC, TensorFlow Probability; (d) Variational autoencoders — neural networks that learn generative models by maximizing ELBO; (e) Gaussian process regression — approximate posterior over function space for scalable GP inference; (f) Sensor fusion — approximate joint posterior over multi-sensor states when exact fusion is intractable.
